Participants' click error plotted as Z-scores relative to a permuted null (Y axis) across auditory cue timing conditions (X axis) by gaze-contingent termination condition (individual lines). Each line represents a different gaze-contingent termination as labeled in the To determine whether hazard localization was better than expected if participants were not using video-specific scene information, and whether this effect differed across conditions, we analyzed click-error z-scores using a 3x3 repeated-measures ANOVA with cue timing and gazecontingent termination as within-participant factors. As seen in Figure 2, the model error differed significantly from zero, (F(1, 33) = 995.45, p < 0.0001), indicating click errors were significantly lower than under the permuted null distribution. This suggests that, across conditions, participants used scene information to localize the hazard, resulting in better hazard localization performance.

Click Permutation

The ANOVA also revealed a significant main effect of cue timing, (F(2, 66) = 23.598, p < 0.0001), such that localization improved as the auditory cue was presented closer to hazard onset. This pattern is consistent with the fact that later cue times provide participants with more task-relevant information by showing video closer to hazard onset, as hazards evolve and become more distinct and recognizable to observers over time.

Following the significant main effect of cue timing, Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons were conducted. Z-scores differed significantly between all times such that the closer cue timing is to hazard onset, the more precise the localization was compared to a permuted null (full table of pairwise comparisons in Supplementary Materials). Overall, these results suggest that as the scene unfolds, more task relevant information is present for observers to use for more accurate localization of hazards.

There was a significant main effect of gaze-contingent video termination condition, (F(2, 66) = 9.398, p < 0.001) suggesting attentional resources were, as expected from the literature with static images and stimuli, presaccadically allocated towards the target object, as shown by improved localization precision. However, there was no significant interaction between cue timing and gaze-contingent video termination condition, (F(4, 132) = 1.163, p = 0.33), indicating that this effect of saccadic attentional shifts was related to when participants made saccades, rather than when the hazard became dangerous in the stimulus videos.

Following the significant main effect of the gaze-contingent video termination condition, Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons were conducted. Z-scores differed significantly between covert attention and overt attention conditions (Mdiff = 0.63, SE = 0.15, 95% CI = [0.25, 1.01], p <0.0001), such that participants more accurately localized hazards if they were able to fixate the target of their saccade before the video was removed from the screen, compared to covert attention alone. The difference between the covert attention condition and presaccadic attention condition was not significant (Mdiff = 0.27, SE = 0.13, 95% CI = [-0.06, 0.60], p = .139), nor was the difference between presaccadic attention and overt attention (Mdiff = 0.36, SE = 0.16, 95% CI = [-0.04, 0.77], p = .09), suggesting localization accuracy using presaccadic attention is somewhere between covert attention and overt attention.

Overall, results from the Z-scored click errors suggest an improvement in accuracy with additional hazard relevant scene information as well as eye movement information, in line with a presaccadic attention account.

Landing position error permutation

Figure 3 participants' saccade landing error decreased with cue time (F(2,66) = 15.31, p < 0.0001), such that the closer the cue was to hazard onset, the more they looked towards the hazard compared to the null distribution of saccade landings. Additionally, there was a significant main effect of gaze-contingent video termination condition (F(2, 66) = 4.243, p= 0.0185), however, there was no interaction between the conditions (F(4, 132) = 1.132, p = 0.3445), suggesting that differences in accuracy of reported hazard position were driven by better saccade planning across some of the termination conditions.

To identify differences between levels in the gaze-contingent video termination condition, pairwise comparisons with a Bonferroni correction (critical alpha = 0.0167) were performed for all unique comparisons in the termination condition. Pairwise comparison between presaccadic attention and covert attention Z-scores showed a significant difference between the conditions (Mdiff = 0.462, SE = 0.155, 95% CI = [0.070 0.853], p = 0.0164), suggesting presaccadic attention supported more accurate saccades compared to covert attention alone. Conversely, comparison between overt attention and covert attention Z-scores showed no significant difference between the conditions (Mdiff = 0.166, SE = 0.137, 95% CI = [-0.1803, 0.5114], p=0.7077); similarly, no significant difference was found between overt attention and presaccadic attention conditions (Mdiff = 0.296, SE = 0.18, 95% CI = [-0.748, 0.156], p = 0.3252).

Overall, the overt attention z-score results suggest that later cue timing not only improved observers' explicit reports of hazard location but also improved initial gaze guidance toward the hazards. Additionally, differences in landing error between gaze-contingent video termination conditions support an account of presaccadic attention's role in helping direct saccadic eye movements.

Discussion

Here, we aimed to address a gap in the literature concerning whether presaccadic attention, which had been previously reported only in experiments which used static, isolated, stimuli, could be observed in dynamic stimuli which more closely resembled real-world environments. Using a video-based gaze-contingent paradigm, we demonstrated that, similar to previous work with static images, observers are better able to localize target objects if they have begun to plan a saccade, but that that this improvement, which we argue is a presaccadic shift of attention, does not bring task performance to the level achieved by fixating the target.

While previous research has shown information acquired during presaccadic attentional shifts can be used outside of basic feature discrimination, and provides object selective input (Wolfe & Whitney, 2015; He & Kowler, 1991; Vishwanath & Kowler, 2003), such that it may allow for object-form information within scenes (Castelhano & Pereira, 2018), these studies did not explore complex naturalistic stimuli, much less moving naturalistic stimuli. Using our gazecontingent video termination paradigm, with a hazard localization task, we demonstrated that information gathered during presaccadic attention is task informative to a degree between covert attention (peripheral vision) and overt attention (first fixation) regardless of saccade latency, aligning with this previous work with static images. Our findings support an account of presaccadic attention serving localization functions prior to fixation.

Notably, this role of presaccadic information was not linked to changes in how much task-relevant information was available in the scene prior to and during saccade planning. At least in our task, additional attentional resources allocated during a saccadic eye movement increased precision in hazard localization, but this was not dependent on whether the hazard itself had become obvious in the video, pointing to a tightly bounded temporal effect linked to the saccade itself. As previously described, presaccadic attention is operative in a narrow window immediately prior to the saccade itself (beginning, at most, 150ms prior), and our results suggest that information prior to this short presaccadic window is not a substantial factor.

However, our method only probed spatial precision, and future work in dynamic scenes could investigate whether presaccadic attention improves representational detail (as previously reported with isolated or crowded objects; e.g., Wolfe and Whitney 2014).

Our results are in line with the limited static scene literature on presaccadic attention (Castelhano & Pereira, 2018) which showed no interaction between scene-object context consistency and improved object processing at presaccadic object preview. More recent work on how feature level and object level processing progresses as the eye movement unfolds suggests presaccadic attention improves visual acuity (Kwak et al., 2023). This work builds on prior work with the aforementioned static images demonstrating that presaccadic attention improves spatial precision (Vishwanath & Kowler, 2003) and reduces crowding (Wolfe & Whitney, 2014) at the location of an impending saccade prior to the eye movement. It is likely that all of these effects are part and parcel of the benefits of presaccadic shifts of attention, and that these effects are likely quite spatially specific around the saccade target (Greenwood et al., 2017), rather than representing an increase in attention to the entire scene (Castelhano & Pereira, 2018).

Overall, our results extend our understanding of presaccadic attention, pushing into the context of dynamic, evolving, scenes for the first time, and show the characteristic change in localization accuracy across covert attention, presaccadic attention and overt attention conditions. We do not claim that these results are particularly unexpected on their face, as one would expect saccade planning processes to be the same regardless of stimuli, but it remains necessary to test and validate our assumptions about how these systems behave in environments which more closely approximate the world outside the laboratory. Future work here could investigate other well-established questions in this space, including whether the target of the impending saccade is represented in more detail and, if this is the case, whether it is represented as features or objects, although there are considerable challenges to doing this with natural video.

To assess whether differences in click error between the gaze-contingent video termination conditions were influenced by saccade latency, we fitted two linear mixed-effects models to the condition-level z-score data. In both models, the dependent variable was the mean hazard-localization z-score for each participant in each auditory cue timing and gaze-contingent video termination condition. Auditory cue timing and gaze-contingent video termination condition were entered as categorical fixed effects, mean post-cue saccade latency for first saccade towards video was entered as a continuous fixed effect, and participant was included as a random intercept. The first model included only main effect of saccade latency, whereas the second model also included an interaction between saccade latency and gaze-contingent video termination condition. Neither model showed a significant main effect of saccade latency or a significant interaction involving saccade latency. Accordingly, these analyses are reported in the Supplementary Materials.

To examine whether differences in localization performance reflected more accurate saccade planning rather than differences in visual information use, we repeated the primary analyses using overt attention mean z-scores per unique level as the dependent variable. This included a 3x3 repeated measures ANOVA across auditory cue timing and gaze contingent video termination condition including an interaction between the conditions, as well as a separate ANOVA restricted to the hazard-onset cue condition.
